claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Herrmann et al., 1990 and Bergsland et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Sox2 is known to be expressed in neural progenitors that form the NT where it contributes to maintain their undifferentiated state.
claims.source: Sox2 is known to be expressed in the neural progenitors that form the NT where it contributes to maintain their undifferentiated state.
claims.evidence: Draws from established knowledge about Sox2 function in neural development.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of Sox2 in cells of the PSM is sufficient to reprogram these cells to adopt a neural identity.
claims.source: Its involvement in the neural specification has also been revealed by a study showing that ectopic expression of Sox2 in cells of the PSM is sufficient to reprogram these cells, which then adopt a neural identity (Takemoto et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Takemoto et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Bra protein was initially identified for its essential function in the formation of the paraxial mesoderm during the posterior extension phase.
claims.source: Bra protein was initially identified for its essential function in the formation of the paraxial mesoderm during the posterior extension phase (Herrmann et al., 1990; Wilson et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Herrmann et al., 1990 and Wilson et al., 1995.

claims.claim: In chimeric mouse embryos composed of both Bra mutant and wild-type cells, only wild-type cells are capable of generating posterior mesoderm.
claims.source: Its crucial role in mesodermal specification has been demonstrated, in particular, by phenotypic study of chimeric mouse embryos composed of both Bra mutant and wild-type cells, and in which only wild-type cells are capable of generating posterior mesoderm (Wilson and Beddington, 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Wilson and Beddington, 1997.

claims.claim: Sox2 and Bra are expressed in posterior progenitors of developing embryos, indicating that activation of their expression takes place in progenitor cells before these cells colonize the NT or the PSM.
claims.source: More recent studies have shown that Sox2 and Bra are expressed in posterior progenitors of developing embryos, indicating that activation of their expression takes place in progenitor cells before these cells colonize the NT or the PSM (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012; Wymeersch et al., 2016; Martin and Kimelman, 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012; Wymeersch et al., 2016; Martin and Kimelman, 2012.

claims.claim: Both Sox2 and Bra proteins are co-expressed in progenitor cells.
claims.source: In addition, these studies have shown that both proteins are co-expressed in progenitor cells, an observation consistent with the presence of bi-potent progenitors in this tissue.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and consistent with the concept of bi-potent progenitors.

claims.claim: Mouse progenitors display regional differences in Sox2 and Bra expression levels with regions of higher Sox2 in the PZ being neural-fated, and those with higher Bra being mesoderm-fated.
claims.source: Importantly, it has been found that mouse progenitors display regional differences in Sox2 and Bra expression levels with regions of higher Sox2 in the PZ being neural-fated, and those with higher Bra being mesoderm-fated (Wymeersch et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Wymeersch et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Bra and Sox2 influence the choice between neural and mesodermal lineages by their antagonistic activities on the regulation of neural and mesodermal gene expression.
claims.source: Works done in mouse embryos and in in vitro systems derived from embryonic stem cells indicate that Bra and Sox2 influence the choice between neural and mesodermal lineages by their antagonistic activities on the regulation of neural and mesodermal gene expression (Koch et al., 2017; Veenvliet et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Koch et al., 2017 and Veenvliet et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Cells of the PZ contribute to formation of the presomitic mesoderm (PSM) and the neural tube (NT).
claims.source: The use of fluorescent tracers in bird and mouse embryos has revealed that cells of the PZ, called here posterior progenitors, contribute to formation of the presomitic mesoderm (PSM), the mesodermal tissue that generates muscle and vertebrae but also of the neural tube (NT), the neuro-ectodermal tissue that gives rise to the central nervous system (Selleck and Stern, 1991; Iimura et al., 2007; Wilson and Beddington, 1996; Psychoyos and Stern, 1996).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies using fluorescent tracers in bird and mouse embryos.

claims.claim: Resident posterior progenitors have the capacity to self-renew while providing new neural and mesodermal progenies.
claims.source: Grafting experiments next showed that resident posterior progenitors have the capacity to self-renew while providing new neural and mesodermal progenies (Cambray and Wilson, 2002; McGrew et al., 2008), thus indicating that the PZ contains progenitors of different tissues.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous grafting experiments by Cambray and Wilson, 2002 and McGrew et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Retrospective clonal analysis studies in mouse embryo revealed the existence of single progenitors giving rise either to neural or mesodermal cells, and bi-potent progenitors (NMPs) that generate both neural and mesodermal cells.
claims.source: Heterogeneity in the progeny of PZ cells was further confirmed by retrospective clonal analysis studies performed in the mouse embryo which revealed the existence of single progenitors, giving rise either to neural or mesodermal cells, but also of bi-potent progenitors, named neuro-mesodermal progenitors (NMPs), that generate both neural and mesodermal cells (Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous clonal analysis study by Tzouanacou et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The existence of bi-potent progenitors has been shown at earlier stages of zebrafish development and in bird embryos.
claims.source: The existence of bi-potent progenitors has since been shown at earlier stages of zebrafish development (Attardi et al., 2018) and in bird embryos (Solovieva et al., 2020; Wood et al., 2019; Guillot et al., 2021) (for reviews Wymeersch et al., 2021; Sambasivan and Steventon, 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in zebrafish and bird embryos.

claims.claim: High levels of Sox2 give cells low motile properties and make them integrate the NT.
claims.source: Our data support a model in which high levels of Sox2 give cells low motile properties and make them integrate the NT while high levels of Bra rather give them high motile and diffusive properties that push them to exit the PZ and integrate the PSM.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data from overexpression and time-lapse imaging experiments.

claims.claim: High levels of Bra give cells high motile and diffusive properties that push them to exit the PZ and integrate the PSM.
claims.source: Our data support a model in which high levels of Sox2 give cells low motile properties and make them integrate the NT while high levels of Bra rather give them high motile and diffusive properties that push them to exit the PZ and integrate the PSM.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data from overexpression and time-lapse imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Progenitors co-expressing Sox2 and Bra at comparable levels move with an intermediate speed and remain resident of the PZ as this tissue is moving posteriorly.
claims.source: Located in-between these low and high motile/diffusive cells are progenitors co-expressing Sox2 and Bra at comparable levels, that are moving with an intermediate speed and remain resident of the PZ as this tissue is moving posteriorly.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing different motility levels based on Sox2/Bra ratios.

claims.claim: While graded expression of Sox2/Bra confers a higher short-term stability in PZ shape, random distribution provides a higher rate of elongation, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
claims.source: Indeed, while graded expression of Sox2/Bra confers a higher short-term stability in PZ shape, random distribution provides a higher rate of elongation, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling comparing different spatial distribution patterns.

claims.claim: The gradient pattern provides stability by limiting local and transient deformations.
claims.source: Taken together, by exploring and comparing Sox2/Bra spatial distributions, our modeling data indicate that while the gradient pattern provides stability by limiting local and transient deformations, random distribution of cell-to-cell heterogeneity could promote cell rearrangements, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling comparing different spatial distribution patterns.

claims.claim: Random distribution of cell-to-cell heterogeneity could promote cell rearrangements, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
claims.source: Taken together, by exploring and comparing Sox2/Bra spatial distributions, our modeling data indicate that while the gradient pattern provides stability by limiting local and transient deformations, random distribution of cell-to-cell heterogeneity could promote cell rearrangements, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling comparing different spatial distribution patterns.

claims.claim: Brachyury plays a role in cell migration.
claims.source: It has been shown that Brachyury plays a role in cell migration (Wilson et al., 1995; Wilson and Beddington, 1997; Turner et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Brachyury function.

claims.claim: Mouse cells that have a mutation in the Brachyury gene have lower migration speed than wild-type cells when isolated and cultured.
claims.source: In particular, mouse cells that have a mutation in the Brachyury gene have lower migration speed than wild-type cells when isolated and cultured, explaining part of the mouse embryonic axis truncation phenotype (Hashimoto et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Hashimoto et al., 1987.

claims.claim: A rise of Sox2 expression promotes the transition of posterior progenitors to NT during chick embryo secondary neurulation.
claims.source: Although a role for Sox2 in the control of progenitor cell migration has, to our knowledge, not previously been reported, recent works have demonstrated that a rise of Sox2 expression promotes the transition of posterior progenitors to NT during chick embryo secondary neurulation (Kawachi et al., 2020) and that turning off Sox2 is necessary for NMP to enter the mesoderm in zebrafish embryo (Kinney et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Kawachi et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Turning off Sox2 is necessary for NMP to enter the mesoderm in zebrafish embryo.
claims.source: Although a role for Sox2 in the control of progenitor cell migration has, to our knowledge, not previously been reported, recent works have demonstrated that a rise of Sox2 expression promotes the transition of posterior progenitors to NT during chick embryo secondary neurulation (Kawachi et al., 2020) and that turning off Sox2 is necessary for NMP to enter the mesoderm in zebrafish embryo (Kinney et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Kinney et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The dorsal zone between the PZ and the NT does not display excessive cell migration but rather local cell intercalations.
claims.source: In addition, it has also been observed by time-lapse analysis that the dorsal zone between the PZ and the NT does not display excessive cell migration but rather local cell intercalations (Roszko et al., 2007; Gonzalez-Gobartt et al., 2021a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous time-lapse studies by Roszko et al., 2007 and Gonzalez-Gobartt et al., 2021a.

claims.claim: Posterior progenitors undergo an epithelial-mesenchymal transition before reaching their full potential to give rise to progeny in the NT and the PSM.
claims.source: In line with this explanation is the fact that during the course of axis elongation posterior progenitors undergo an epithelial-mesenchymal transition before reaching their full potential to give rise to progeny in the NT and the PSM (Guillot et al., 2021; Goto et al., 2017; Dias et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Guillot et al., 2021; Goto et al., 2017; Dias et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Physical constraints exerted by neighboring tissues, in particular the PSM, promote the posterior movement of the PZ.
claims.source: Several works, performed in bird embryo, have indicated that physical constraints exerted by neighboring tissues, in particular the PSM, promote the posterior movement of the PZ (Bénazéraf et al., 2017; Bénazéraf et al., 2010; Xiong et al., 2020; Regev et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on physical constraints in bird embryos.

claims.claim: Differential adhesion between progenitors could regulate their segregation.
claims.source: One interesting possibility that is taken into account in our mathematical models is that, as it has been demonstrated during NT dorso-ventral patterning (Tsai et al., 2020), differential adhesion between progenitors could regulate their segregation.
claims.evidence: Speculative possibility based on previous work by Tsai et al., 2020 on differential adhesion in NT patterning.

claims.claim: Fluid-like state and disordered cellular movements have been described in PSM tissue to be key for zebrafish embryo axis elongation and morphogenesis.
claims.source: Interestingly, this fluid-like state as well as disordered cellular movements have been described in PSM tissue to be key for zebrafish embryo axis elongation and morphogenesis (Lawton et al., 2013; Das et al., 2017; Mongera et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on PSM tissue properties in zebrafish.

claims.claim: The PZ is able to regenerate after partial ablation.
claims.source: Several studies have shown that this particular region of the embryo is able to regenerate after partial ablation (Joubin and Stern, 1999; Yuan and Schoenwolf, 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous ablation studies by Joubin and Stern, 1999 and Yuan and Schoenwolf, 1999.

claims.claim: Spatial cell-to-cell heterogeneity appears to be an enabling factor for self-correction in the PZ.
claims.source: Spatial cell-to-cell heterogeneity, which allows easier re-organization of remaining cells than graded cell pattern, thus appears to be an enabling factor for self-correction.
claims.evidence: Inferred from modeling results showing better shape conservation with random distribution.

claims.claim: Spatial heterogeneity in gene and protein expression is a common trait of living systems and has been observed in many contexts including early mouse embryos or cancer cells.
claims.source: Spatial heterogeneity in gene and protein expression is a common trait of living systems and has been observed in many contexts including, early mouse embryos or cancer cells (Prasetyanti and Medema, 2017; Fiorentino et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on cellular heterogeneity in different biological contexts.

results.result: Sox2 and Bra proteins are co-expressed in all PZ cells of quail and chicken embryos at stages HH5-11, with high cell-to-cell heterogeneity in their relative levels. This heterogeneity is characterized by intermingled cells displaying high Sox2/low Bra, high Bra/low Sox2, or equivalent levels of both proteins, contrasting with the homogeneous expression in adjacent NT and PSM tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide converging evidence from immunodetection experiments across multiple embryos (n=8 for quail, confirmed in chicken) and developmental stages (HH5-11). The observations are consistent, well-documented with appropriate sample sizes, and supported by visual evidence in Figure 1. The comparison to adjacent tissues (C4) provides important context validating the specificity of heterogeneity to the PZ.

results.result: Sox2 and Bra protein levels change along putative cell trajectories from the PZ to differentiated tissues, with Sox2 increasing and Bra decreasing along the neural path, and the opposite pattern along the PSM path. Cell-to-cell heterogeneity is driven more by Sox2 variation (CV=41.8%) than Bra variation (CV=30.75%), and while some spatial enrichment exists (Sox2high anteriorly, Brahigh posteriorly), heterogeneity is present throughout the entire PZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C12 are supported by quantitative measurements from 7-9 embryos with clear statistical analysis. The coefficient of variation calculations (C9) provide rigorous quantification of heterogeneity. The spatial analysis (C11-C12) appropriately acknowledges both regional enrichment and widespread heterogeneity, avoiding overinterpretation of the gradient pattern.

results.result: Manipulating Sox2/Bra ratios through overexpression or downregulation controls PZ cell exit and tissue destination. High Bra or low Sox2 promotes exit to PSM, while high Sox2 or low Bra promotes exit to NT, with cells largely depleting from the PZ in all manipulation conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 are supported by functional experiments with appropriate controls, adequate sample sizes (n=21-28 embryos per condition), and statistical testing. The bidirectional manipulations (gain and loss of function) provide strong evidence. However, the authors acknowledge potential overestimation of NT signal in Bra overexpression due to medial PSM cell localization, showing appropriate caution in interpretation.

results.result: PZ cells exhibit high motility with diffusive, non-directional movement patterns. Raw motility and posterior directionality of PZ cells exceed those of PSM and NT cells, while corrected motility shows PZ cells move as fast as PSM cells and faster than NT cells. Within the PZ, Sox2high cells are less motile than Sox2-negative cells, and cell movements are diffusive as demonstrated by linear MSD.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 are supported by rigorous time-lapse imaging analysis across 7 embryos with 538 PZ cell trajectories. The distinction between raw and corrected motility appropriately accounts for tissue-level movements. The MSD analysis (C23) provides quantitative evidence for diffusive motion. The Sox2 reporter experiment (C22) directly links protein expression to motility, though sample size (n=5) is modest.

results.result: Sox2 and Bra regulate PZ cell motility in opposite directions: Bra overexpression increases motility without affecting directionality, while Sox2 overexpression decreases motility and introduces anterior bias. Bra downregulation reduces motility and shifts directionality anteriorly, while Sox2 downregulation shows no significant effect on motility or directionality.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by time-lapse imaging of electroporated embryos with adequate sample sizes (n=5-7 embryos, 234-874 trajectories per condition). The asymmetry in effects (strong for Sox2 overexpression and Bra knockdown, weaker for Bra overexpression and Sox2 knockdown) is acknowledged and discussed. Statistical testing appears appropriate, though the 'tendency' noted in C27 suggests borderline significance.

results.result: The effects of Sox2 and Bra on PZ cell motility occur independently of differentiation, as neither Pax6 (neural marker) nor Msgn1 (mesodermal marker) is induced 7 hours after Sox2 or Bra overexpression, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 are supported by immunodetection and in situ hybridization at an appropriate early timepoint (7 hours) when motility effects are measurable but before differentiation. This temporal analysis strengthens the conclusion that motility regulation is a direct effect rather than a consequence of differentiation. However, the sample sizes (n=5-9 embryos) are modest, and the analysis is limited to two markers.

results.result: A mathematical agent-based model incorporating Sox2/Bra-dependent motility, adhesion, and proliferation recapitulates key biological properties including stable PZ cell numbers, increasing NT/PSM cells, cell motility patterns, and non-directional movement. The model demonstrates that both random motion and adhesion/non-mixing properties are essential for tissue integrity, and simulated Sox2/Bra perturbations reproduce experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 describe a computational model that successfully captures experimental observations. The model validation against multiple experimental parameters (cell numbers, motilities, directionality) and perturbation experiments strengthens confidence. However, as with all models, it relies on assumptions about parameters and mechanisms (e.g., adhesion, non-mixing) that are not all directly validated experimentally. The model is appropriately presented as supporting rather than proving the biological mechanisms.

results.result: Computational modeling comparing random, gradient, and mixed Sox2/Bra spatial distributions reveals that random distribution provides faster elongation, more posterior movement of resident progenitors, better conservation of PZ shape over time, and higher diffusivity (MSD) compared to gradient distribution. The gradient pattern provides short-term stability by limiting transient deformations, while random distribution promotes cell rearrangements, tissue fluidity, and long-term shape conservation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 and C55-C57 present modeling predictions comparing different spatial distribution patterns. The predictions are internally consistent and follow logically from the model structure. However, these are computational predictions that lack direct experimental validation. The biological system appears to use a 'mixed' pattern, which shows intermediate properties, but the specific functional advantages of randomness versus gradient remain theoretical predictions rather than experimentally demonstrated facts.

results.result: The authors propose a model where high Sox2 levels confer low motility causing cells to integrate into the NT, high Bra levels confer high motility causing cells to exit to PSM, and intermediate Sox2/Bra levels result in intermediate motility allowing cells to remain resident in the posteriorly-moving PZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 represent the central mechanistic model synthesizing the experimental findings. This model is well-supported by the convergence of expression data (C1-C12), functional perturbations (C13-C18, C24-C27), and motility measurements (C19-C23). The model provides a coherent explanation for how cell-to-cell heterogeneity in transcription factor levels translates into differential cell behaviors and tissue destinations.

results.result: Prior work has established that Sox2 and Bra are key transcription factors for neural and mesodermal specification, respectively, that they are co-expressed in posterior progenitors before cells colonize NT or PSM, that regional differences in their expression correlate with cell fate, and that they influence lineage choice through antagonistic regulation of neural and mesodermal gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C47 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These background claims provide essential context for the current work. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations of prior findings are consistent with the cited work. However, as these are literature claims, their validity depends on the accuracy of the cited studies, which are not independently evaluated here.

results.result: Previous studies using fluorescent tracers, grafting experiments, and clonal analysis have established that PZ cells contribute to both PSM and NT formation, that resident progenitors can self-renew while producing neural and mesodermal progeny, and that the PZ contains both uni-potent and bi-potent (NMP) progenitors in multiple vertebrate species.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 accurately summarize key prior findings about PZ cell properties with appropriate citations spanning multiple model organisms and experimental approaches. This background establishes the biological context and heterogeneity of the progenitor population that motivates the current study.

results.result: Prior work has shown that Brachyury plays a role in cell migration (with Bra mutant cells showing reduced migration speed), that Sox2 expression changes are associated with progenitor transitions to NT in chick and mesoderm entry in zebrafish, that the dorsal PZ-NT boundary shows local cell intercalations rather than extensive migration, and that posterior progenitors undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition during axis elongation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 accurately cite relevant prior work connecting Sox2/Bra to cell behaviors and developmental transitions. These citations appropriately support the discussion of mechanisms and provide context for interpreting the current findings. The characterizations of prior work appear accurate based on the citations provided.

results.result: Prior work and theoretical considerations suggest that physical constraints from neighboring tissues promote PZ posterior movement, that differential adhesion may regulate progenitor segregation, that fluid-like states and disordered movements are important for morphogenesis in related systems, that the PZ can regenerate after ablation, and that spatial heterogeneity in gene expression is common in biological systems and may enable self-correction and robustness.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C69 draw on prior literature and extend it with speculation about mechanisms and broader implications. C64, C66, C67, and C69 are well-supported by citations. C65 is explicitly speculative ('interesting possibility'). C68 is an inference from the modeling results. These claims appropriately distinguish between established facts, speculative mechanisms, and implications of the current work.
